items.title: Al Letson challenged a conservative activist on voter fraud. He abruptly ended the interview.
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708550-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
items.content:
Readers, this week, you’re in for two firsts: the show’s first full-length video episode and its first guest to angrily storm off mid-interview. 

While interviewing conservative activist J. Christian Adams, host Al Letson challenged his claims of widespread voter fraud in the US—a claim that’s been widely debunked. After 13 minutes of back and forth, Adams abruptly left the interview, a moment that you can see right

here on our Instagram page.

Don’t worry, this week’s episode isn’t 14 minutes long.

national voting rights correspondent Ari Berman swooped in at the eleventh hour. We even got Berman’s take on Adams’ quick departure:

“If he feels so confident in his numbers and arguments, why would he be so defensive from the very beginning to extremely basic and fair questions that you were asking? You weren’t asking him gotcha questions. You were asking him very basic questions to defend his assertions, and he immediately got so defensive. It reminded me of President Donald Trump storming off

when Kristen Welker pushed him on the 2020 election."

But this episode is so much more than Adams. In it, Letson and Berman take a serious look at Adams’ and the Trump administration’s claims of voter fraud, their lack of evidence, and how they’re using these claims to rig the upcoming midterm elections. Trust me, it’s an episode you won’t want to miss.

items.title: I won’t let my legal briefs do the talking
items.author: 1axbipo1irgzb0g5p0jb9p2t006x8r6vwo6ztv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Now is not the time to hide. It is the time to stand tall and speak out.

That is the message I have delivered at a series of events over the past few weeks. I have spoken to diverse audiences of business leaders, lawyers, students and concerned citizens.

At each event, I was warmly received. People praised my work as a lawyer and as a vocal opponent of Donald Trump’s efforts to subvert democracy.

Yet when I called on the audience to act and speak out, I too often heard the usual concerns: “I am just one person.” “My friends are MAGA.” “My clients or customers won’t like it.”

I recently sat down with Semafor for an interview about Democracy Docket. The host noted that most lawyers prefer to let their legal briefs do the talking. Why, he wanted to know, don’t I follow that same approach?

My answer was the same one I gave my audience: it is too dangerous to stay silent.

It is true that the future of free and fair elections is playing out in courthouses across the country. But it is not enough for lawyers to litigate. They have an obligation to speak publicly and plainly about these cases.

This is not a new frustration for me. For years, I have watched Republican lawyers take center stage promoting election-denial conspiracy theories while those charged with defending democracy hide behind their legal filings.

During the Biden presidency, this disagreement spilled into public view when some in the White House criticized me for “fighting on every possible front — filing a flurry of lawsuits and exerting public pressure through the media.”

Since Trump’s return to power, those critics have largely gone quiet. Yet too few people are willing to take on Trump directly, without caveats or false equivalence.

Meanwhile, I have redoubled my efforts. I have continued to litigate, arguing in federal and state courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court last term.

My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in 41 states. They include some of the most consequential cases for the future of democracy and free and fair elections. The firm is also preparing for what may come next: post-election litigation, recounts and election contests.

Even so, I refuse to stop speaking out. I won’t simply let my legal filings do the talking.

items.title: Who will stop Trump now from seizing voting machines?
items.author: 1axb2a54qx7g67d6wvvnght97tmq66zafeh1ur@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Convicted criminal and former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters is pushing a scheme to give the Trump administration control over voting machines. In August, she called on the Department of War “to go in and demand to have these machines in their custody.”

More recently, her lawyer, election denier Peter Ticktin, suggested that Peters’ plan was to “get control over the ballots as soon as the machine spits them through and then do a recount.” And on Oct. 5, according to Trump ally Ed Martin, Peters met with Trump in the Oval Office to discuss election security.

We have been here before.

In December 2020, a group of conspiracy theorists sat in the Oval Office arguing that Donald Trump should declare a national emergency and order the secretary of defense to “seize, collect, retain and analyze” voting machines, equipment and electronically stored election information.

The motley crew of election deniers pushing this approach included attorney Sidney Powell, Trump’s former national security adviser Michael Flynn and former Overstock.com CEO Patrick Byrne. The day before the meeting, Flynn had suggested that the president could invoke martial law and use the military to “rerun” elections in swing states.

More important than who advocated seizing voting equipment was who opposed it. The White House counsel, his deputy and the staff secretary all helped stop Trump from signing the order. So did Attorney General William Barr. Even Rudy Giuliani opposed using the military.

Those guardrails no longer exist.

items.title: Action Alert: Speak Out Against Taxpayer-Funded Political Ads
items.author: bounce_75b4552d-49c3-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
This administration’s “flood the zone” strategy continues with actions that raise serious concerns about constitutional principles and the rule of law. As disheartening as these actions can be, we must meet them with informed engagement and expectations for a better future.

Today, we are issuing our latest Action Alert, asking the public to speak out against the misuse of federal resources for partisan political promotion. 

The administration recently spent nearly $12 million in taxpayer funds on television ads promoting the President, with millions more allocated under a $20 million contract for additional ads selected to run during major broadcasts in the critical weeks before the midterm elections. Following widespread criticism, the President announced that the remaining ads would be paid for via his MAGA Inc. Super PAC.

Both approaches raise serious questions under federal law, including restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for unauthorized publicity or political propaganda, the Hatch Act, and federal campaign finance laws. Shifting the payment method from taxpayer funding to privately raised Super PAC funds does not eliminate the need to comply with applicable legal restrictions. 

Our Action Alert outlines four steps you can take today.

LDAD is grateful to our many volunteers who continue to help document important developments, raise concerns, and defend the rule of law. They do this in a variety of ways, for example:

LDAD volunteer, Professor Mark Gordon, recently moderated an important election-related program co-sponsored by the Minnesota State Bar Association and LDAD entitled: Rules and Procedures for Voting in the Midterm Elections in MN.

Lawyers Defending American Democracy

P.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

It hasn’t been an easy year for religious freedom. Across the country, politicians are pushing religious doctrine into public schools and government, while the Supreme Court continues to reshape the constitutional protections that have guided this work for generations.

But thanks to supporters like you, no matter the moment, Americans United will always show up and take action whenever and wherever we can.

In Arkansas, our legal team secured a permanent injunction blocking a law that would have required every public school classroom and library to display a government-chosen version of the Ten Commandments. In Texas, 28 families represented by AU and our allies have asked the Supreme Court to stop a similar law. Across the country, we’re helping students, parents, teachers, and federal workers understand their rights and know what to do when they’re threatened.

This work takes persistence. It takes attorneys who know how to build a case, advocates who know how to move lawmakers, organizers who can unite us, and a community of supporters who make it possible for Americans United to keep showing up.

If you have money set aside in a donor-advised fund, consider using it to support Americans United. Your generosity keeps this work moving forward at a time when it matters deeply.

Thank you for being part of this movement.

With gratitude, Americans United

items.title: Trump is doing family separation but without the backlash
items.author: delivery_20261008060502.47827077.141@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
Children are almost always treated with special deference in American law, because lawmakers understand and respect the significance of adolescence and the necessity of parental guidance. President Donald Trump has upended this long-standing, universal understanding in a particularly insidious way during his second term. For the first time in our nation’s history, tens of thousands of children are being separated from their parents, who, at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are being violently arrested inside of the country, then detained, and quickly deported without their kids. These children are essentially left to fend for themselves or are placed with an unknown caregiver, which in some cases has led to horrific endings. Although this may sound awfully similar to Trump’s 2018 “zero-tolerance” policy, it is worse, because there is no explicit family separation policy this time around, making it harder to challenge in court. Instead, family separation has become just another devastating consequence of the president’s mass deportation agenda.

Under past administrations, ICE policy held that any detainees who were parents should be reunited with their children before being deported, or agents must get confirmation that there is a designated caregiver in place for their children in the parents’ absence. Last year, upon Trump returning to the White House, ICE revised this policy to make it only applicable “when operationally feasible,” which gave agents all the leeway they needed to ignore the historical guidance in order to prioritize mass deportations. “This loosening of guidelines, combined with scaled-up immigration enforcement, has resulted in the detention of thousands of parents, many of whose minor children are U.S. citizens,” a recent analysis by the Migration Policy Institute concluded.

Under Trump 2.0, the Department of Homeland Security no longer provides reliable data on its immigration enforcement, but the Brookings Institution estimates that as of April 2026 about 205,000 children have likely experienced a parental detention since Trump began his second term and about 145,000 of these children are U.S. citizens. Mothers in particular seem to be affected, with ProPublica finding that the Trump administration is deporting about four times as many moms of U.S. citizen children per day as the Biden administration did, most of whom have minor or no criminal histories at all. 

Stories of these children are playing out across the country, like in Minnesota, where three children have been separated from their father for nearly 10 months after he was yanked out of his car and violently arrested on his way to work. And in Alabama, where one woman has been caring for an old co-worker’s 2-year-old for nearly a year since ICE picked up the baby’s mother while she was on a grocery run. In Illinois, a college senior found himself the sole breadwinner of his family after ICE arrested and detained his uncle. Three sisters in San Francisco were among a lucky few who were reunited with their mother after she was detained for almost a year, leaving the eldest sibling to take care of the household while juggling college classes and navigating a complicated immigration system for her mother.

Then there are the children who ICE arrests with one or both of their parents. Although the U.S. government has historically allowed families to remain in detention together, the Trump administration has quietly been separating children by giving their parents false promises that they’ll be able to stay in touch with them. In reality, as detailed by Mother Jones, oftentimes children are sent to the Office of Refugee Resettlement and reclassified as unaccompanied minors—they are not; the U.S. government knows their parents are in detention—and sent off to live with foster parents. ORR does not track these types of cases, so it's unclear how many children are being reclassified, but Mother Jones estimated they now make up a “huge chunk” of ORR’s caseload. Under normal circumstances, unaccompanied minors are defined as children who arrive at a U.S. border alone, with no parent or guardian. 

Regardless of how the Trump administration chooses to manipulate immigration law, the National Immigration Law Center says parents and legal guardians who are detained by ICE have a legal right to make decisions about their minor child’s care. They are also allowed to see their children while in detention, upon written request, whether that’s in person or over a video or phone call. And if a parent faces deportation, they also have a legal right to make decisions about what happens to their children, which usually comes down to either allowing the child to remain in the U.S., regardless of the child’s immigration status, or to be deported alongside the parent. All of these decisions are supposed to happen with a lawyer, but even this is no longer happening, due to financial constraints, the administration’s attacks on legal aid for minors, and its extreme hostility toward immigrants, leaving parents with little to no recourse when ICE does not follow protocol. 

Children do not get to choose their parents’ immigration status, yet their families are being torn apart over it. The consequences are clear, with studies showing that children who lose a parent to sudden, forced deportation experience anxiety, anger, aggression, isolation, and depression. It also often leads to housing instability, academic withdrawal, and family dissolution. Yet, the president is unbothered by this; in fact, he’s doubled down on efforts to eliminate immigrant children from the U.S. altogether, evidenced by his birthright citizenship executive order. Despite the Supreme Court categorically rejecting it earlier this year, Trump has since introduced yet another executive order targeting birthright citizenship.

The Trump administration’s assault on immigrants has been cruel at every turn, but what it’s doing to immigrant children could be its worst act by far.

None of this is an accident. When President Donald Trump returned to office, he set out to build an army ahead of the midterms — one that would answer to him and only him.

items.title: Cleta Mitchell and Tina Peters want Trump’s commerce secretary to seize voting machines
items.author: 1axbtb211adycvi3lnnbh4ao4et20n3l42bbab@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Convicted election denier Tina Peters reportedly met with President Donald Trump this week in the Oval Office to discuss plans for the midterms. Details of the meeting are scarce, but lately Peters has been pushing the president to take action to intervene in the midterms.

Specifically, Peters wants Trump to pressure Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to exploit an executive order Trump signed in his first term related to protecting U.S.-made technology, by using it to seize voting machines.

  • Peters and other election deniers are pushing the conspiracy that voting machines use parts from China, Russia and other foreign countries that make them vulnerable to hacking.
  • On his online show, former Trump DOJ official Ed Martin said Peters discussed this conspiracy with Trump, which was recently boosted by Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Peters has been pushing Trump to take action to control voting for the midterms and laid out a step-by-step plan for what the president can do — starting by declaring the security of voting machines a national security issue.
  • “The president is taking it seriously,” Martin said. “If Congress won’t pass the SAVE America Act — and they won’t — then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do. It’s not a local issue when it’s national security. And it’s clearly national security.”

It’s not a new scheme — Peters first floated this plan over the summer — but the renewed push from her and other prominent election deniers as Election Day nears is worrisome.

Conservative lawyer Cleta Mitchell is pushing the same plot.

  • “Lots of people are asking [Trump] to declare a national emergency to protect against the vulnerabilities of electronic voting systems,” Mitchell explained on social media. “It turns out that [Trump] already declared such an emergency in May 2019.”
  • That 2019 order declared a national emergency because of the threat of foreign adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in information and communications technology. The order banned transactions involving foreign-owned manufacturers that “present threats to the security or resiliency of critical infrastructure.”
  • Mitchell and Peters think voting machines qualify as critical infrastructure — and that Lutnick has the power to act.

items.title: I'm tired
items.author: 1axbyk38xej0d18t2ecbxu21xrsuzaz6b7eajn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
These last few weeks before an election are always the worst. The stress and uncertainty hang over everything we do like a dense fog. We can predict a wave. We can anticipate victories and defeats. But we don't really know what will happen.

And every election has surprises. Sometimes they are welcome. Other times they are soul-crushing.

I have worked on campaigns that have won and campaigns that have lost. I was there when Democrats retook the House and Senate in 2006 and when, in Barack Obama's words, we took a "shellacking" in 2010. I was devastated in 2016 and found new hope in 2020.

Yet this election feels different. I tell myself this is what the final weeks of an election always feel like, but I don't really believe it.

The truth is that the stakes of this election, and the threats facing it, are much higher than in any election I've worked on. The President of the United States is personally trying to suppress voting rights. His administration is exploring ways to subvert the results.

This means the work of lawyers — my work — has never been more critical. Yet big law firms are nowhere to be seen. Small firms like mine are carrying the load.

As of this morning, my firm is litigating 83 voting and election cases in 41 states. These are not side skirmishes. These are fights in which we are on the front lines, representing clients whose right to free and fair elections is under attack.

I've spent the last few weeks on the road, flying from coast to coast. This morning, I woke up at 7 a.m. to an inbox full of legal briefs ready for review. Then I gave a talk to a group of lawyers and recorded a podcast before checking my email again on the way to the airport.

I'm writing this on a plane heading back to the East Coast. When I land, there will be more legal work and another speech in New York City.

I remind myself that I will eventually make it back to my home outside of Washington, D.C. I’ll eventually see my dog, Blue. If I'm being entirely honest, I'm just very tired.

But I keep going, because the fate of democracy is on the line. We can’t sit this fight out.

I go to court because that is my duty as a lawyer. I speak out because I am a citizen.

Donald Trump is trying to subvert our elections because he wants to keep power. He has built an entire movement around election denialism and voter suppression. And now democracy itself is under threat.

I have said before that it is not enough for any of us — including lawyers — to simply do our jobs. We must all speak out. Democracy Docket is how I do that.

items.title: "Take a look at California": Trump's roadmap for attacking the midterms
items.author: 1axcfkrug2ymtkj60fzi5wuzhttvq41xmj44u7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
On Monday afternoon, a reporter asked Donald Trump why, if he was so worried about fraud, he was telling his supporters to vote by mail. Trump said he had "no choice because a lot of people want to vote by mail."

He then launched into his usual baseless allegations of fraud. Pressed to say where this fraud had taken place, he told reporters to "start off by taking a look at California."

With the midterms less than a month away, we have become sadly accustomed to Trump's false attacks on free and fair elections. But his focus on California is more than routine. It is both a decade-long fixation and a roadmap for his plans in 2026.

Weeks after winning in 2016, Trump blamed "serious voter fraud" in California for his loss of the popular vote by nearly 3 million votes. He has repeated the charge in every election cycle since.

In 2019, he claimed California had "admitted to a million [illegal] votes" in a court settlement. It hadn't. In 2020, his false claims about California's mail ballots earned him Twitter's first-ever fact-check label on one of his posts. In 2024, he told Dr. Phil that "if Jesus Christ came down and was the vote counter, I would win California."

This year, the rhetoric has escalated into action. Trump has called California "one of the most dishonest states" and told Fox News that its "mail-in votes are a fraud."

On June 5, three days after the state's primary, Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, announced that his office was conducting "multiple election fraud investigations." Weeks later, Trump bragged that he had personally phoned the "U.S. attorney in California" with a request: "Do me a favor. Take a look."

Around the same time, Jay Clayton, then the U.S. attorney in Manhattan, went on CNBC to question California's voting rules, claiming they created "an opportunity for fraud." Days later, Trump nominated him to be director of national intelligence.

Trump's obsession with California isn't just about the fact that he has repeatedly lost the state in landslides, or that it is reliably controlled by Democrats. It's that he sees California as the biggest obstacle to stopping a Democratic wave in November.

items.title: DOJ sued over ‘unprecedented’ 1,000 election monitors plan
items.author: 1axbnezgbzmewvzims5q6ccil8e099oygqqke7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
• The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) today threw out two pro-voter decisions in cases related to Washington’s legislative redistricting, sending them back to a lower court for new proceedings in light of the Court’s decision earlier this year in Louisiana v. Callais.
  • That was the ruling that gutted the Voting Rights Act. Monday’s decision was the latest evidence that the landmark civil rights law is now essentially useless for stopping racial gerrymandering.
  • A federal judge allowed the state’s new ban on using student IDs for voting to remain in place for this fall’s general election. But the judge also barred the state from enforcing a directive that prohibits state election officials from accepting a student ID as a valid form of identification to vote.
  • That means: If a voter has no other way to prove their identity to vote, an election official can still consider a student ID as part of the evidence that he or she is qualified to vote.
  • Still, the complexity and confusion could act as another barrier to voting for students, who already face more than their share of hurdles.
  • A federal judge is set to rule on Trump’s effort to use vast amounts of Americans’ personal data to create state-by-state lists of people eligible to vote in federal elections, after being fully briefed on the legal arguments for and against Trump’s “State Citizenship Lists.”
  • The decision is a victory for disability advocates who argued that the requirements increased the likelihood that valid ballots cast by those with difficulty getting to a physical polling place would be rejected on technicalities.
  • In a Fox News interview, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito, one of Trump’s staunchest allies on the Court, rejected the growing chorus demanding reforms at the high court, saying the current justices are actually victims of intimidation.
  • Alito said Democrats’ calls to expand the Court are a political attempt to influence the justices’ decisions.

items.title: This time, take Trump literally
items.author: 1axchqbo0ons8c114rd9dx657actsnmxj6kctf@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Earlier this year, The New York Times asked Donald Trump whether he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines in swing states after the 2020 election. His answer was chilling: "Well, I should have."

Trump is telling us what he plans to do in this year's midterms. He is trying to rig the elections and subvert their results. While we have been able to stop him so far, there is no guarantee that we will continue to prevail in the weeks ahead.

Yet despite the obvious signs of Trump's plan, too many reporters and pundits downplay it. They adhere to the false neutrality that has come to dominate legacy media coverage over the last decade.

No phrase captures this attitude more clearly than the admonition to take Trump seriously but not literally. The suggestion is that only out-of-touch elites pay attention to his actual words. Real voters — and those in the media who claim to speak for them — know to focus on his vibes.

When it comes to voting and elections, this advice has been catastrophically wrong. In 2020, Trump's words before the election were prophetic about what he would do afterward. His refusal to concede foreshadowed the attack on Jan. 6, 2021.

Trump is once again in power, and he is again telling us his plan. He has weaponized the entire federal government — including the Department of Justice and the U.S. Postal Service — to make voting more difficult.

He is threatening to deploy federal agents at the polls and to disrupt voting. And he is reaching for every other tool of election rigging: partisan gerrymandering, restrictions on voter registration, attacks on mail-in voting and the use of bogus lists to purge eligible citizens from the rolls.

But most dangerous is what he has been saying for more than a year about the counting, tabulation and certification of election results. Despite what the U.S. Constitution says, he has repeatedly claimed the power to direct this process.

This is not a new idea. It has been his plan all along.

items.title: You've stood with me. Here's what's next.
items.author: 1axbkddtc87p0ndwzoslnw6i979x1i1ymvs1ib@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Election Day is 30 days away, and the fight for free and fair elections is here. In some states, early voting has already begun, and nearly every state has sent out mail-in ballots.

I have been on the road the last week traveling. I apologize that some of my essays have been shorter and videos less well-produced.

For months, we have been building toward this moment. Campaigns are communicating with voters and executing get-out-the-vote plans. Nonprofit groups are registering voters and recruiting poll workers.

Then there are the lawyers. My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in more than 40 states. We have beaten the Department of Justice more than 20 times, defended voting by mail against Trump's executive orders, and won three times at the Supreme Court to keep Missouri from using an illegally gerrymandered map.

But that is only part of the fight.

Democracy Docket is tracking almost 200 cases in nearly all 50 states and D.C. Keeping a spotlight on what is happening to democracy in the courts is a critical part of the effort to protect our elections.

Since Trump returned to office, Democracy Docket has closely tracked his authoritarian schemes. While other media outlets have bent the knee, Democracy Docket has remained unbowed.

I created Democracy Docket for moments like this. And you, our readers, have been with me the entire time.

When I'm tired, your words energize me. Your support helps me fight another day. I will never forget that.

No matter what happens on Election Day, and no matter what Trump does or threatens, I promise you this: Democracy Docket will keep fighting.

As a subscriber, you know that everything on the Democracy Docket website and in its flagship newsletters is available to everyone. All its reporting and video content is free.

What you may not know is that Democracy Docket also offers a premium membership for people who want deeper analysis. Premium members receive my exclusive analysis and are invited to member-only briefings and events.

Most importantly, premium members sustain Democracy Docket's independent, pro-democracy mission. It has no corporate parent or investors. There are no venture capitalists or private equity backers. It does not rely on ActBlue or Substack.

To put it simply, it relies on you.

With Election Day right around the corner, we will have to work harder than ever. If you haven't upgraded to a premium membership, please consider doing so today. Become part of the community that powers Democracy Docket's work and protects our democracy.

If now isn't the right moment for you, I understand, and I thank you for being a loyal reader. Every one of you is an important part of our team and of this mission.

We are all in this fight together, and I couldn't do it without you. We have an important fight ahead in just 30 days, but I know we will win — together.

items.title: America’s latest electoral fault line: Israel
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708488-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
items.content:
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took the stage at the United Nations last month, diplomats streamed for the exits. Three years after October 7, when much of the Western world rallied behind Israel in the wake of Hamas’ attack, the political ground has shifted.

Some of the biggest changes are happening here in the US. Two years ago, Abbas Alawieh helped lead the Uncommitted movement, pressuring Democrats over Gaza. Now he’s running for Michigan state Senate, and Kamala Harris is calling him. Elsewhere in Michigan, AIPAC and its allies spent close to $30 million backing Abdul El-Sayed’s opponent in the Democratic Senate primary. El-Sayed won anyway.

For some voters, the prominence of Israel itself is striking.

“I don’t know why Israel has become the pivotal point,” said Mimi Price-Miletic, a Democratic voter in Michigan. “There are so many issues in this country that we should be dealing with, and you’re worried about what’s happening, like, millions of miles away?”

And the divide crosses party lines. Younger Republicans are questioning US support for Israel, even as party leaders advance deeper defense cooperation. 

Meanwhile, AIPAC faces new challenges to its influence, as younger Jewish political groups, like J Street and Jewish Voice for Peace, offer sharply different visions for what should come next.

, reporter Najib Aminy follows the new fault lines forming around the US–Israel relationship and asks: As the old political consensus is tested, who gets to shape what replaces it?

items.title: Why top Texas election denier Ken Paxton could cause chaos if he loses his Senate race
items.author: 1axb4tfa76e59b2esfskm9005uz0lpny82asbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
It’s October, Halloween is coming, and I can’t think of anything more frightening than the enormous federal resources that Trump has directed to try to prove that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him. (OK, maybe “The Blair Witch Project” or “The Exorcist” are scarier — but at least those are only movies).

Luckily, the horror show that is the Trump administration’s effort to find mass voter fraud and relitigate the 2020 election has fallen flat. With all the chaos and noise Trump and his allies are creating around the midterms, it’s easy to forget that the election deniers are losing.

But this week was a good reminder: Not one, but two Trump administration officials tasked at least in part with proving 2020 voter conspiracies abruptly resigned — and both quit without proving anything. First was Kurt Olsen, a hardcore Trump loyalist who led a special White House task force probing 2020 election conspiracies, then moved to the Department of Justice.

The other was Andrew Bailey, a former Missouri attorney general and avowed election denier, who was the FBI's co-deputy director and helped lead the bureau’s raid on a Fulton County, Georgia election hub earlier this year.

They’re the latest in a string of resignations of administration appointees who were brought in to prove 2020 election conspiracy theories, or indict the president’s political enemies, and utterly failed to do so. Nearly half a dozen election deniers recently resigned — and there’s still no evidence that the 2020 election was rigged.
